title: S3 in Depth: Storage Classes, Versioning, and Security

questions.prompt: What is the general trade-off across S3 storage classes?

options.text: Cheaper storage generally means higher or slower retrieval
Cheaper storage always means faster retrieval
They differ only in durability
The classes are identical in every way

questions.explanation: All classes share eleven-nines durability, but the cheaper the storage tier, the higher or slower the retrieval — so you match the class to access frequency and needed speed.

questions.prompt: Which storage class is best when access patterns are unknown or changing?

options.text: S3 Glacier Deep Archive
S3 Intelligent-Tiering
S3 One Zone-IA
S3 Standard-IA

questions.explanation: Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between access tiers based on usage, which fits unpredictable or changing access patterns.

questions.prompt: How does S3 versioning protect against an accidental overwrite?

options.text: It blocks all writes
It keeps the previous version so you can restore it; deletes add a delete marker
It emails you before every change
It converts the object to Glacier

questions.explanation: With versioning on, an overwrite creates a new version while retaining the old one, and a delete adds a delete marker — so accidental changes are recoverable.

questions.prompt: Which are good ways to keep S3 data secure? Select all that apply.

options.text: Leave Block Public Access on and grant access with scoped policies
Share single objects via time-limited presigned URLs
Use SSE-KMS when you need audit and access control over the keys
Make the bucket public so anyone can read it

questions.explanation: Keep buckets private, share narrowly with presigned URLs, and use SSE-KMS for auditable key control. Making the bucket public is the classic leak.

questions.prompt: A rule that automatically transitions objects to cheaper classes and deletes them after a set age is called a ____ rule.
questions.explanation: A lifecycle rule transitions and/or expires objects based on age, cutting cost without manual intervention.

questions.prompt: Why should versioning be paired with a lifecycle rule that expires old versions?

options.text: Otherwise versioning stops working
Old (noncurrent) versions keep accumulating and cost storage, so expiring them controls the bill
Lifecycle rules disable versioning
It is required to make the bucket public

questions.explanation: Versioning retains every overwrite, so noncurrent versions pile up. A lifecycle rule expires them to keep storage costs from growing unbounded.
